story.headline: Antonelli wins Monza from 19th
story.summary: Kimi Antonelli won the Italian GP at Monza from 19th on the grid, catching team-mate Russell late and stretching his F1 title lead to 66 points.
story.display_body: Kimi Antonelli, the 20-year-old Italian in his second Mercedes season, produced one of the drives of the year at his home Grand Prix: starting 19th after a difficult qualifying, he carved through the field and reeled in his own team-mate George Russell in the closing laps to win at Monza. Max Verstappen (Red Bull) took third ahead of the McLaren pair of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, with Lewis Hamilton sixth for Ferrari. The win stretches Antonelli's lead in the drivers' championship (the season-long points title for individual drivers) to 66 points over Russell, with Hamilton a distant third, 76 points back, after the season's 13th round.
story.why: A 66-point cushion is not yet mathematically decided, but it is commanding — and the manner of it (winning from 19th, at home, against his nearest rival) is the kind of statement that tends to break a title race open rather than tighten it. A young driver is on the verge of a first world championship.

story.headline: Lugano make it six from six
story.summary: FC Lugano beat Basel 3-1 away for a sixth win in six games and returned to the top of the Swiss Super League, three points clear with a game in hand.
story.display_body: Two wins in four days took FC Lugano to a perfect six victories from six games and back to the top of the Swiss Super League. On Thursday (3 Sep) new signing Albian Ajeti struck in the 94th minute for a 1-0 home win over Servette; on Sunday (6 Sep) Lugano fell behind at Basel, then turned it around to win 3-1, helped by a bad error from Basel goalkeeper Mirko Salvi. Lugano now sit on 18 points with a goal difference of +13, three clear of Young Boys — and, because Bern have already played seven games to Lugano's six, the leaders also hold a game in hand (a fixture not yet played that a rival has). The rest of the round underlined the shift: St. Gallen won 2-0 at Servette to leave the Geneva club bottom, while Sion beat Thun 2-1 with a late goal. For context, Lugano are one of the league's smaller, lower-budget clubs; Basel, by contrast, are among Swiss football's traditional heavyweights and have now lost twice at home already this season, sitting only fifth.
story.why: The Swiss title race is being led from an unfamiliar place. Lugano's start is the best in the division, and a modest side setting the pace over the wealthier names is exactly the kind of early-season story that decides where the pressure lands come winter.

story.headline: Arsenal edge Chelsea to stay top
story.summary: Arsenal came from behind to beat Chelsea 2-1 and stay perfect at the top of the Premier League, level on points with Manchester City.
story.display_body: The reigning English champions passed their first big test of the new season. Chelsea, who spent roughly £349m in the summer transfer window, led inside two minutes through Morgan Rogers, but Arsenal replied through Kai Havertz (25th minute) and a Martin Ødegaard winner just after half-time (50th) to win 2-1 at the Emirates. It is three wins from three for Arsenal, who reach nine points and stay top — level on maximum points with Manchester City, whose own perfect start continued at the weekend. Chelsea have now lost one of their opening three despite the outlay.
story.why: Two of the pre-season favourites are already pulling clear at the top, and the result is a small early marker that Arsenal's title-winning group has not gone soft — while it raises the familiar question of whether spending big buys an instant team at Chelsea.

story.headline: Leclerc crashes out at Monza
story.summary: Charles Leclerc was knocked out of Ferrari's home Italian GP in a heavy crash and taken for medical checks, with Hamilton only sixth.
story.display_body: There was no home celebration for Ferrari, the Monza crowd's team. Charles Leclerc was pitched out of the race in a heavy crash and was taken for further medical checks afterwards, while team-mate Hamilton could finish only sixth — a chastening afternoon in front of the tifosi (Ferrari's fervent Italian fans). It caps a season in which Ferrari have slipped well off the championship pace.
story.why: Monza is the one race Ferrari most want to win, and crashing out of it is the sort of low that fuels the recurring questions about the team's direction and whether it can build a car to fight at the front again.

story.headline: AfD wins Saxony-Anhalt election
story.summary: The far-right AfD won Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election on 6 September with about 43.9%, far ahead of the CDU's 17.2%, but every rival rules out governing with it.
story.display_body: The far-right AfD (Alternative für Deutschland) won Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election on Sunday 6 September by a wide margin, taking about 43.9% of the vote — roughly 39 of the 87 seats — against 17.2% for the governing CDU (Christian Democratic Union), according to the state returning officer's official preliminary count. It is the AfD's strongest result yet in any German state and more than doubles the CDU's share in a region the CDU had led since reunification. The SPD (9.3%), Greens (8.9%), Left (8.6%) and the new left-populist BSW (5.3%) trailed far behind. AfD co-leader Alice Weidel called the outcome "a clear mandate" to form a government and predicted Chancellor Friedrich Merz would be gone by Christmas — but every other party in the state parliament rules out governing with the AfD, which Germany's domestic-intelligence agency classifies as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organisation, so despite finishing first the AfD has no realistic path to a governing majority. Coalition talks among the mainstream parties are only now beginning.
story.why: a far-right party clearing 40% in a German state is a threshold event for post-war German politics and a direct blow to Merz's federal CDU nine months into his chancellorship; it sharpens the debate over the "firewall" that has kept the AfD out of power and reverberates across a Europe already watching hard-right gains.

story.headline: Israeli strikes kill 11 in south Lebanon
story.summary: Israeli air strikes on Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon early on 7 September killed at least 11 people, including two children and two medics, despite the 2024 truce.
story.display_body: Israeli air strikes on the town of Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon early on Monday 7 September killed at least 11 people, including two children and two medics, and wounded several more, Lebanon's official National News Agency (NNA — the state wire service) reported. A warplane hit a residential building, killing nine there, while further strikes struck the wider Nabatieh district. It is the deadliest single day in a run of Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon over the past month — the NNA-reported toll of these incidents has climbed from around four killed on Sunday 6 September to seven in mid-August and now eleven — all carried out despite the November 2024 ceasefire that formally ended the Israel–Hezbollah war. Israel says it targets Hezbollah fighters and infrastructure; Monday's casualties, which Lebanese authorities describe as civilians and rescue workers, were not independently reconciled with that account.
story.why: the strikes keep eroding a truce that is nominally still in force, and the mounting civilian toll raises the risk of the fragile Lebanon front reopening.

story.headline: Von der Leyen visits Greenland with EU package
story.summary: Von der Leyen arrived in Nuuk on 6 September for a two-day visit, pledging a substantial EU investment package as Trump presses for US control of the Danish Arctic territory.
story.display_body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen arrived in Greenland's capital Nuuk on Sunday 6 September for a two-day visit, pledging a "substantial" EU investment package as US President Donald Trump keeps pressing for American control of the Danish Arctic territory. She was received by Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and the package — expected to run to hundreds of millions of euros — targets critical minerals, satellite communications and renewable energy, alongside a promise of closer political ties. Greenland, home to about 57,000 people, left the then-European Community in 1985 but its residents remain EU citizens through Danish nationality. Trump has repeatedly said the US "needs" the mineral-rich island for national security, citing — without evidence, DW notes — a supposed Chinese and Russian naval presence; both Copenhagen and Nuuk have rejected his demands.
story.why: the visit is a pointed European counter to Washington's annexation talk, testing whether the EU can offer Greenland enough to keep an increasingly contested Arctic aligned with Europe rather than under US pressure.

story.headline: Zelensky sees war lasting into winter
story.summary: Zelensky said on 7 September the war looks set to continue into winter after US envoys Witkoff and Kushner's shuttle diplomacy produced no announced breakthrough.
story.display_body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday 7 September that Russia's war looks set to continue into the winter, after the latest round of US-led diplomacy produced no announced breakthrough. His comments followed talks in Kyiv with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who had met President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin two days earlier; the Kremlin called that meeting "constructive," but the shuttle mission ended without a ceasefire or a concrete framework. Meanwhile Russian regional officials said Ukrainian drone strikes killed at least two people and injured several in the Perm and Belgorod regions overnight.
story.why: it is the clearest signal yet that the Witkoff–Kushner initiative — the most active US peace push in months — has stalled, leaving the front line and the strikes on both sides unchanged as a third winter of full-scale war approaches.

story.headline: Nepal mourns 1,300 flood dead
story.summary: Nepal held a national day of mourning on 7 September for the more than 1,300 people killed in the 26 August Himalayan glacial-lake flood, as bodies were still being recovered.
story.display_body: Nepal held a national day of mourning on Monday 7 September for the more than 1,300 people killed in the Himalayan glacial-lake flood that struck on 26 August, as search teams kept recovering bodies 13 days on. Buddhist monks performed rituals for the dead in the hard-hit Nuwakot district, and many victims are being buried in mass graves — a practice that has distressed relatives still waiting for the thousands reported missing to be identified. The toll has risen steadily since the disaster, from about 270 in the first days to over 1,000 by early September and past 1,300 now, with rescue and recovery work continuing across the flood zone.
story.why: it is among the deadliest disasters in Nepal's recent history, and the scale of the loss — driven by a glacial-lake outburst of the kind climate scientists warn is becoming more frequent in a warming Himalaya — is only now becoming fully clear.
